result.summary: The Messenians rise in a second war against Sparta in the 39th year after Ithome fell. Pausanias dates it, Aristomenes is made king and dedicates a shield in Sparta, and the Spartans receive Tyrtæus from Athens. The armies then gather with allies at Boar's Memorial.

scenes.title: Dating the second war
scenes.summary: Pausanias gives the year of the revolt and argues from Tyrtæus which Spartan kings reigned, rejecting Rhianus' claim about Leotychides.

scenes.title: Deræ and Aristomenes' shield
scenes.summary: The first battle at Deræ is indecisive, but Aristomenes' bravery wins him kingship and command. He slips into Sparta by night and hangs a shield in the temple of Athene.
scenes.stakes: Aristomenes risks capture and death inside enemy Sparta.

scenes.title: Tyrtæus sent from Athens
scenes.summary: Following a Delphic oracle, the Spartans ask Athens for an adviser. The Athenians send the lame schoolmaster Tyrtæus, who recites his verses to the Spartans.
scenes.stakes: Sparta's chance of winning depends on obeying the oracle; Athens fears disobeying the god.

scenes.title: Armies gather at Boar's Memorial
scenes.summary: Both sides muster allies at Boar's Memorial near Stenyclerus, named from a covenant of Hercules with the sons of Neleus.
scenes.stakes: Each side risks defeat in a pitched battle.

alias_notes.explanation: Athene of the Brazen House, Sparta's patron goddess.

notable_quotes.reason: Tyrtæus' line on the first war's length, used to date the second.
Aristomenes' bold inscription defying Sparta in its own temple.

analysis.text: Pausanias reasons about chronology using Olympiad dates, Athenian archons, Spartan king lists and the poet Tyrtæus as evidence.
The passage shows courage and divine guidance: Aristomenes' daring contrasts with Sparta's reliance on an oracle.

legacy.text: Tyrtæus' war poems became a model of martial verse, and his name is used for poetry that urges soldiers on.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias dates the revolt to the 23rd Olympiad, about 685 BC, using the Olympic victor list.

language_notes.text: Dating by Olympiad: Greeks counted years in four-year cycles from the first Olympic games; the stadium race winner named each Olympiad.
Athens named each year after its annual archon, a chief magistrate, so this gives a second dating system.
'Third generation' counts from the fathers' war: those who fought it, their sons, then the present generation, matching Tyrtæus' 'fathers of our fathers'.
'Preterhuman' means beyond what is natural to humans, superhuman.
The first clause is obscure: Aristomenes seems to mean he would let none disown, that is deny honour to, any man valiant in war.
Anapæsts are verse in a marching rhythm, suited to rousing soldiers; elegiac verses are in couplets.
A covenant 'over a boar's entrails' refers to a sacrifice in which the entrails sealed an oath.

context_notes.text: Athene Chalciœcus ('of the Bronze House') was Sparta's chief goddess, with a bronze-clad temple on the acropolis.
Tyrtæus became famous for war poems that inspired Spartan courage; the tradition of him as a lame schoolmaster is ironic.
The Great Goddesses are Demeter and Persephone, honoured in the Eleusinian mysteries near Athens.

literary_notes.text: The nighttime dedication in the enemy's temple shows Aristomenes' daring and flair for psychological warfare.
Athens obeys the god yet sends an apparently foolish, lame man; the unlikely helper proves the oracle's good adviser.
